RELIGION CORNER Innocent and inconvenient By Pastor Jim Hopkins “Certainly this man was innocent.” Luke 23:47b In Luke’s gospel Jesus speaks from the cross three times. His courageous words are: • “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” • (To one who was crucified with him) “Truly, I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” • “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Following his last cry he breathed his last and one of the Roman soldiers who had carried out the crucifixion declared, “Certainly, this man was innocent.” The soldier’s declaration echoes through history a witness to Jesus fundamental goodness as does the reality that this innocent one was, and is, very inconvenient to many. He was inconvenient to the Temple authorities who feared his popularity. He was inconvenient to Pontius Pilate who feared he would lead a popular uprising. He was inconvenient to Herod Antipas who feared him as a potential rival. He was inconvenient to the crowd that feared standing up to the powers that be in order to support him. He is inconvenient to many of us for he represents a God who suffers, a God we are not sure that we want. In her book “God In Pain: Teaching Sermons on Suffering,” Barbara Brown Taylor speaks to this inconvenient reality, “Christianity is the only world religion that confesses a God who suffers. It is not a popular idea, even among Christians. We prefer a God who prevents suffering, only that is not the God we have got. What the cross teaches us is that God’s power is not the power to force human choices and end human pain. It is, instead, the power to pick up the shattered pieces and make something holy out of them – not from a distance, but right close up.” Jesus is inconvenient because, rather than preventing suffering, he suffers with us and bids us to “take up your cross and follow me.” This is not a message of popular appeal. This is not the promise of wealth, prestige and security. This is not a gospel of prosperity. This is not a theology of self-improvement. This is not cheap grace. This is a costly, demanding, heart-rending, heart-changing way. articles.text: Kids will have a chance to climb up in Public Works’ big trucks, complete a tree-themed art project, and maybe win a new book to take home at Piedmont’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration, hosted by Piedmont Public Works and the Piedmont Park Commission. The event will take place on Thursday, April 24, from 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The annual event, which dates back to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. • • • This year’s event will feature: Public Works big trucks: Works staff uses daily in their work to keep Piedmont’s trees and public spaces healthy and beautiful. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the trucks. Arts & crafts: Park Commissioners will be on hand to assist little ones with their creations. Owl naming contest: A photo exhibit and naming contest will highlight raptors living in Piedmont Parks, including a nesting pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. ComChildren will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of Public Works’ trucks. munity members can share name suggestions online in advance at piedmont.ca.gov/ DracenaOwls. • Raffle: Kids can enter to win a Lego set or children’s book related to Arbor and Earth Day themes. New this year, a raffle for adult attendees will offer an opportunity to take home a California native plant for your garden. • Electric leaf blower demos: Gas powered leaf blowers are not allowed in Piedmont, but clean, quiet electric alternatives can get the job done. Try one for yourself at the event. The event will also include informational tables from the Piedmont Fire Department and the City’s Sustainability Division. Heritage Trees announcement The Arbor Day celebration will also feature the announcement of the 2025 class of Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its seventh year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. This year, the City received nine nominations for Heritage Trees. articles.text: Come to Cat town and meet Pluto and Mars. Meet 1-year-old Pluto and 4-year-old Mars, a playful and affectionate bonded pair of boys looking for a home together. These best friends love to wrestle, chase toys, and even eat and nap together. As shy cats, they’ll benefit from a patient adopter who’ll give them time to feel safe. They thrive in a calm, quiet home, and once they settle in, each has uniquely adorable traits you’ll quickly fall in love with. Mars, a white and brown tabby, asks for affection with headbutts or by gently brushing up against your legs as he walks by. He’s known for using these approaches to flirt with visitors, before flopping over and rolling away. This charming boy also loves scrambling after toys. Although a bit more reserved, Pluto, an orange tabby, is often the first to explore, moving through his surroundings with quiet curiosity. He loves to stalk after his toys, and is a true cuddle buddy, eagerly curling up in a familiar lap for a gentle petting session. Want to meet this duo? Complete an Adoption Inquiry form for a free matchmaking appointment, or book a visit to meet all of Cat Town’s adoptable cats at their cat cafe, located at 2869 Broadway in Oakland. articles.text: The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program is offering grants of up to $6,000 for community-based projects that help prevent stormwater pollution and improve the health of local watersheds, creeks and the San Francisco Bay. Eligible projects include litter reduction efforts, public outreach and education about clean water issues, public art installations and stormwater detention initiatives. One past recipient is I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary, a group of water sports enthusiasts who use their skills and equipment to organize cleanups in areas of the Oakland-Alameda Estuary that are otherwise inaccessible by foot. Other grant-funded projects have included the removal of microplastics from Albany Beach, a cleanup of Sausal Creek in Oakland, and the production of a short film titled Doing Our Part to Clean Up San Francisco Bay. articles.text: Piedmont resident Jean Hansen will be showing her garden for the third time in this year’s Garden Tour. The award-winning Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour returns Saturday and Sunday, May 3–4, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., inviting community members to explore more than 50 water-conserving native plant gardens across Alameda and Contra Costa counties. In addition to showcasing native gardens, 25 of the homes will also participate in a Green Home Showcase, featuring ecofriendly technologies such as solar panels and battery systems, induction stoves, and electric heat pumps. This year’s tour includes the garden of Piedmont resident Jean Hansen. Her landscape, designed to complement her rustic 1912 home, is filled with California native plants that provide food and shelter for local bees, birds and butterflies. Attendees will learn how to design native gardens with yearround color and interest, support wildlife, reduce water usage, and protect both family health and the environment by gardening without pesticides. The tour also highlights practical steps homeowners can take to electrify their homes and reduce carbon emissions. California native plants are naturally adapted to local soil and climate conditions, making them low-maintenance and water-efficient. They are also more effective than non-native species at supporting native birds, butterflies and other wildlife. As the gardens on the tour demonstrate, native plant landscapes can create a uniquely Californian sense of place. The garden tour is free, but advance registration is required at https://www.bringingbackthenatives.net/. For more information contact Kathy@KathyKramerConsulting.net or call (510) 236- 9558. Jean Hansen’s garden features a plethora of native California plants.

articles.text: Josh Bernstein, a 3-time contestant and proud member of Piedmont High’s class of 1975, achieved local – and briefly national – fame that year with his stirring, second-place portrayal of the Bald Eagle at the Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest. His commitment to the role included a freshly shaven head for aerodynamic realism, and his performance was one of the rare news items to ever make Walter Cronkite laugh on the CBS Evening News. For a teenage bird impressionist, it was the equivalent of winning an Emmy, a Peabody, and possibly a fish. Josh has since traded feathers for floss as a longtime practicing dentist, where he’s spent decades perfecting the beautiful whirring call of the high-speed drill. He’s also been raising a lively flock of his own three children and two grandchildren, including his daughter Mavra, who proudly served as M.C. of the Birdcalling Contest during her senior year at Piedmont High. Back home in the hills of Piedmont, Josh lives among a vibrant avian chorus of owls, crows, whippoorwills, woodpeckers, wild turkeys, and chickens – though none have been brave enough to challenge him to a call-off. When not in the office or the backyard, he’s often out in open water, marathon swimming alongside seagulls, pelicans, and great blue herons, pondering which bird might next be worthy of emulation. Now returning to the Bird Calling Contest as a judge, Josh brings a legendary ear, decades of dedication, and the rare distinction of having once cracked up the most trusted man in television with a birdcall. Let the squawking commence. The 56th Annual Bird Calling Contest poster was designed by PHS student Layla Miguel-Reed. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: The Piedmont community is invited to join the Piedmont High School (PHS) English Department and freshman parent representatives for the Ninth Grade I-Search Celebration and public viewing on Tuesday, April 22, from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Piedmont Middle School multipurpose room. These 15 to 30 plus-page documents represent more than nine weeks of intensive work focused on writing, research, and thoughtful reflection. Every freshman has completed a guided research project as part of the I-Search curriculum, demonstrating their growth as writers, thinkers, and investigators. The projects offer compelling insight into what students are curious about in the world and how they communicate their findings. Each student conducted an interview to deepen their understanding of their chosen topic and form original conclusions. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest Josh Bernstein, a 3-time contestant and proud member of Piedmont High’s class of 1975, achieved local – and briefly national – fame that year with his stirring, second-place portrayal of the Bald Eagle at the Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest. His commitment to the role included a freshly shaven head for aerodynamic realism, and his performance was one of the rare news items to ever make Walter Cronkite laugh on the CBS Evening News. For a teenage bird impressionist, it was the equivalent of winning an Emmy, a Peabody, and possibly a fish. Josh has since traded feathers for floss as a longtime practicing dentist, where he’s spent decades perfecting the beautiful whirring call of the high-speed drill. He’s also been raising a lively flock of his own three children and two grandchildren, including his daughter Mavra, who proudly served as M.C. of the Birdcalling Contest during her senior year at Piedmont High. Back home in the hills of Piedmont, Josh lives among a vibrant avian chorus of owls, crows, whippoorwills, woodpeckers, wild turkeys, and chickens – though none have been brave enough to challenge him to a call-off. When not in the office or the backyard, he’s often out in open water, marathon swimming alongside seagulls, pelicans, and great blue herons, pondering which bird might next be worthy of emulation. Now returning to the Bird Calling Contest as a judge, Josh brings a legendary ear, decades of dedication, and the rare distinction of having once cracked up the most trusted man in television with a birdcall. Let the squawking commence. The 56th Annual Bird Calling Contest poster was designed by PHS student Layla Miguel-Reed. articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center astronomer Gerald McKeegan has a few tips for stargazing, planet-watching and observing points of interest in the night sky. McKeegan co-hosts free telescope viewings every Friday and Saturday evening at Chabot alongside other professional and volunteer astronomers, making the center a go-to destination for skywatchers across the Bay Area. Here’s what McKeegan says to watch for in the coming weeks: • Jupiter and Mars are still visible in the evening sky for the next few weeks. • Around 9:30 p.m., look east • • for a bright, yellowish star— Arcturus, a giant star 37 lightyears away. Arcturus appears in the early spring sky and remains visible throughout the summer. The Big Dipper is easy to spot in the northeastern sky after 9 p.m. This familiar star pattern is part of the constellation Ursa Major, or the Big Bear. Telescope season for globular clusters is beginning. These dense, spherical groups of hundreds of thousands of stars are among the oldest in our galaxy—about 12 billion years old. The clusters orbit • the Milky Way’s center in a region known as the galactic halo. There are roughly 160 globular clusters orbiting our galaxy, and they offer a stunning sight through a telescope. Also visible is the faint constellation Corona Borealis, or the Northern Crown. Known to some Native American traditions as the “Campfire Circle,” it usually goes unnoticed—except this year, when it could make headlines. Within the constellation lies T Coronae Borealis (T CrB), a faint star nearly 3,000 lightyears away. Though it appears as a single star, it’s actually a binary system, with two stars orbiting each other. One of the stars is a white dwarf, a small, dense, extremely hot remnant of a once-larger star. It’s pulling gas from its companion, a red giant. When enough gas accumulates on the white dwarf’s surface, a nova occurs—a nuclear explosion that dramatically increases the system’s brightness. T CrB is expected to undergo such a nova event soon—possibly this spring or summer—for the first time in 80 years. The explosion will cause the star to brighten by a factor of nearly 2,000, making it briefly visible to the naked eye. The event will be tracked by telescopes worldwide as the star brightens in hours and fades slowly over weeks. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. Sky over Chabot Conrad Jung

articles.text: Council Considers Expanded Signage Rules for Yards, Public Spaces The Piedmont City Council on Monday, April 7, held a public hearing and introduced the first reading of an ordinance to update the city’s rules on signage in both residential lawns and public areas. The proposed ordinance, based on recommendations from the Planning Commission’s March 10 public hearing, includes a series of changes aimed at clarifying regulations and streamlining approvals. The council voted unanimously to increase the number of allowable non-commercial signs per property from two to five and approved a list of special city events that can post signs in public rights-of-way. The proposed updates seek to: • Define categories of signage; • Streamline the review process for city-initiated events; • Expand temporary sign locations on public property; • Clarify rules around construction signs; and • Establish enforcement procedures. Residents would be allowed up to five non-commercial signs— such as political, graduation, or nonprofit messages—and one construction sign per contractor or design professional. Non-commercial signs would have a maximum display period of six months. Event signs would need to be removed within 10 days after the event. To ensure compliance with First Amendment protections, “all non-commercial signs are treated the same by the law”. The ordinance also spells out prohibited signs, including those that mimic traffic control devices, animated or moving signs, roof signs, balloons or inflatables, and ground signs over 15 feet tall. The City is also proposing a formal process to allow signage on public property, including Piedmont Park and 801 Magnolia Ave., home to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Signs posted by the City would be exempt from permits and standards. Officials also plan to launch a program to manage signage for city-sponsored events in specific locations. Currently, the Public Works Director can issue permits for signage across Magnolia Avenue at Highland Avenue, at the Piedmont Corporation Yard, and on fencing at city recreation facilities such as Coaches Field, Beach Playfield, Hampton Field, the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the city pool. Proposed updates would add bridge railings near Piedmont Community Hall and other rightof-way areas for approved events. The new list of eligible events includes the Piedmont Food Fest, Oktoberfest, the Pumpkin Patch, Turkey Trot, and Christmas Tree Lot. City Council would review and update this list annually. During the hearing, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier questioned how enforcement would work under the six-month rule. “So I take my sign down after six months and then, two days later, I put it back up…” she asked. “That would be fine,” replied Associate Planner Gopika Nair. Kevin Jackson clarified the city’s approach to enforcement: “The city will not be removing signs from private property. The enforcement there would be sending notice to that property owner that they are not in compliance and requesting that they bring their property into compliance by removing that sign, and then following up through a nuisance if they fail to do that.” Jackson added that the City does remove unauthorized signs from public property and will hold them for retrieval by the original poster. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said he is developing a one-page summary of the proposed signage program. “The idea is that less is more,” he said. “We want to have something that’s simple, that is clear… has locations, has types of events that we would consider, and also sign size that [the Council] would consider and durations that are typical.” Associate Planner Gopika Nair (left), City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, City Attorney Deepa Sharma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Mayor Betsy Smegal-Andersen, Councilmember Jennifer Long, Councilmember Tom Ramsey, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, Deputy City Clerk Lisa Argue, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Residents would be allowed up to five non-commercial signs— such as political, graduation, or nonprofit messages—and one construction sign per contractor or design professional. Non-commercial signs would have a maximum display period of six months. Event signs would need to be removed within 10 days after the event. To ensure compliance with First Amendment protections, “all non-commercial signs are treated the same by the law”. The ordinance also spells out prohibited signs, including those that mimic traffic control devices, animated or moving signs, roof signs, balloons or inflatables, and ground signs over 15 feet tall. The City is also proposing a formal process to allow signage on public property, including Piedmont Park and 801 Magnolia Ave., home to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Signs posted by the City would be exempt from permits and standards. Officials also plan to launch a program to manage signage for city-sponsored events in specific locations. Currently, the Public Works Director can issue permits for signage across Magnolia Avenue at Highland Avenue, at the Piedmont Corporation Yard, and on fencing at city recreation facilities such as Coaches Field, Beach Playfield, Hampton Field, the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the city pool. Proposed updates would add bridge railings near Piedmont Community Hall and other rightof-way areas for approved events. The new list of eligible events includes the Piedmont Food Fest, Oktoberfest, the Pumpkin Patch, Turkey Trot, and Christmas Tree Lot. City Council would review and update this list annually. During the hearing, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier questioned how enforcement would work under the six-month rule. “So I take my sign down after six months and then, two days later, I put it back up…” she asked. “That would be fine,” replied Associate Planner Gopika Nair. Kevin Jackson clarified the city’s approach to enforcement: “The city will not be removing signs from private property. The enforcement there would be sending notice to that property owner that they are not in compliance and requesting that they bring their property into compliance by removing that sign, and then following up through a nuisance if they fail to do that.” Jackson added that the City does remove unauthorized signs from public property and will hold them for retrieval by the original poster. articles.text: Layth Haddawy qualified for the USPA National Championships for a second straight year. Piedmont High junior Layth Haddawy continued his power lifting career at the United States Powerlifting Association National Tested Get Bent’s Spring Break in Oakland on April 5. In the Age 16-17 category at 148 pounds, Haddawy lifted a combined total of 1,085 pounds – 352 pounds in the squat, 248 pounds on the bench press, and a 485- pound dead lift. Haddawy last competed in the USPA National Championships in July, when he had a combined weight of 932 pounds. He increased his squat by 43 pounds, his dead lift 66 pounds, his bench 44 pounds, resulting in his combined weight jumping 153 pounds. But after the National Championships in July, an MRI revealed Haddawy had suffered a fracture in his pelvis. “This was my first time competing since I fractured a part of my pelvis and had to take months off from lifting. I wanted to try and qualify for the National meet and test myself on what I could do after my injury. I wanted to take ambitious third attempts and it resulted in getting a slightly lower total, but I still qualified in the event I wanted to reach,” Haddawy said. After fighting through nagging pain he figured out something was wrong. Testing revealed an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. “At first, I didn’t realize my injury was as big a deal as it turned out to be. I probably made it worse by trying to lift lighter weights and adjust my form to what didn’t hurt. But I realized I wasn’t getting better, so I underwent an MRI. It revealed part of my hamstring muscle tore off a segment of the bone in my pelvis. It happened in August and I didn’t start my rehab until October,” Haddawy said. Haddawy last competed in the 132-pound division, adding 16 pounds to his frame. He thinks the added weight is giving him more power after battling a difficult weight-cut in his previous division. “I’ve been reassured by how stronger I’ve gotten since I’ve come back in a higher weight class. As I got toward the end of competing in the 132 weight class, I was walking around about 6-7 pounds heavier than where I was competing. In 148, I’m walking around just four pounds heavier, so I still have decent room to grow in this weight class,” Haddawy said. The Get Bent’s Spring Break competition officially marked Layth’s one-year anniversary as a competitive power-lifter. “I’ve learned a lot about competing, how to train, what to do, and what not to do. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team closed the Concord Varsity Tournament with a win on Wednesday, April 9, defeating neighboring the Head-Royce Jayhawks 7-5 at Concord High School. That’s when Piedmont scored once in the bottom of the fifth before jumping ahead with a powerful four-run bottom sixth. Piedmont got its first run on a two out rally. LUKE HARRIS Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, just finished his senior season at Carleton College. He finished at the team’s leader in several categories, including 538 points scored, 103 free throws, 200 field goals made, and 914 total minutes. With Harris leading the show, the Knights went 18-10 and reached the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference Finals before losing to Saint Johns of Minnesota. Harris earned All-Conference honors for the third consecutive season, was an All-Region selection by the National Association of Basketball Coaches, and academic All-District. He averaged 19.2 points per game and scored a team-high of 22 in the MIAC Finals. As a sophomore, Harris helped lift Carleton College to the MIAC Conference championship with an 86-76 win over St. Johns where the guard scored 19 points. articles.text: Two-time Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Lynn Nottage’s acclaimed Crumbs from the Table of Joy comes to the Aurora Theatre stage in Berkeley April 26, running through May 10. Directed by Elizabeth Carter, Nottage’s play follows the Crump family as they relocate from Pensacola, Florida, to Brooklyn following the death of the family matriarch. The play is told through the eyes of 17-year-old Ernestine Crump and focuses on the arrival of communist-leaning Aunt Lily, who challenges the family’s dynamics and beliefs. The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. Preview nights are April 26-27, and 29-30. Opening night is Thursday, May 1 at 7 p.m. The play runs through May 10. Two performances per week, Wednesday evenings and Sunday matinees, are mandatory mask-required performances. For all other performances, masks will be encouraged but not required. A streaming of Crumbs from the Table of Joy performances will be streamed online May 20-25 for audiences to enjoy in their homes. Streaming performances will run concurrently with in-person performances. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/crumbs to purchase tickets and view showtimes. Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production of Here There Are Blueberries, written by Moisés Kaufman and Amanda Gronich, continues at the Roda Theatre stage through May 11. The play takes place in 2007 and opens in the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, where a mysterious album featuring Nazi-era photographs arrives at the desk of an archivist. Museum curators begin to unravel shocking truths behind the images and what they reveal about the historical tragedy and our own humanity. Here There Are Blueberries tells the story of these historical photographs and is based on true events. The play was a 2024 Pulitzer Prize Drama finalist and is performed on Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s stage following a run at the Wallis Annenberg in Beverly Hills. Cast includes Scott Barrow, Nemuna Ceesay, Delia Cunningham, Luke Forbes, Barbara Pitts, Jeanne Sakata, Marrick Smith, Grant James Varjas, Anna Shafer and Sam Reeder. Post-show discussions are held following April 18, April 24 and April 29 performances, guided by members of Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s artistic team. articles.text: Opera San Jose (OSJ) will present the Northern California premiere of Hector Armienta’s Zorro this Saturday, April 14, closing out the company’s 41st season. The production stars tenor Xavier Prado as Diego de la Vega and Zorro and soprano Maria Brea as Ana Maria Soza, with Latino stage director David Radamés Toro making his OSJ debut and Conductor Jorge Parodi returning to OSJ after his debut last season on Rigoletto. Armienta’s opera about the famed masked vigilante marries humor and suspense and comes alive with mariachi, flamenco and corrido music. Set in an early 1800s Spanish colony, this new work follows the adventures of a nobleman who defends the poor and enslaved while hiding his true identity behind a black mask. “I can’t wait to bring Zorro to our audiences. This mesmerizing opera blends stunning orchestration with high drama, delivering an enthralling experience for both regular opera-lovers and newcomers to the form,” Opera San José General Director Shawna Lucey said. “From the fierce brass fanfares to the rich strings and sonorous woodwinds, the score pulses with adventure, romance, and suspense. With thrillingly challenging vocals and nonstop momentum, Zorro takes us on a heart-pounding ride.” Xavier Prado as Diego de la Vega and Zorro and soprano Maria Brea as Ana Maria Soza in Opera San Jose’s Zorro Zorro is the second Spanish-language opera to be presented on OSJ’s mainstage following last season’s production of Florencia en el Amazonas. “So many in our community speak Spanish in the home, and we have been delighted to welcome new audiences who are excited to hear works they can instantly follow,” Lucey said, adding that many California public school students study the history of the state and its early settlements, and will gain insight on that era while watching Zorro. “This production will provide an outstanding, and wildly dramatic, look at the political dynamics of that era, making it a great introduction for younger audiences,” she said. The performance will run approximately two hours and thirty minutes with one intermission. Join OSJ staff for a pre-show discussion at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. Zorro is showing on select dates April 19 through May 4. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/zorro to learn more and to purchase tickets.

The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. articles.text: The episodic journey of the Dutton family begins in Ft. Worth, Texas. The year is 1883. It concludes in Montana where James Dutton and family, wife Margret and young son John, settle on the land that will become the Yellowstone Ranch. 1923 is the sequel to 1883, and, like its prequel, it is wonderfully cinematic, a rich production, character-driven, and the writing by Taylor Sheridan is extraordinary. It is also superbly acted (led by Harrison Ford as Jacob Dutton and Helen Mirren in the role of Cara Dutton). Unlike 1883, which is linear, 1923 is comprised of three integrated vignettes, each an evocative, stand-alone story meant to create a compelling context and rich history of that singular year. Season 1 focuses on Spencer Dutton (Brandon Sklenar), Harrison Ford and Helen Mirren in 1923 nephew of Jake and Cara Dutton, veteran of WWI, and now working for the British Protectorate. He has recently arrived in Nairobi where he meets Alexandra (Julia Schloepfer), the reluctant fiancé of a titled Englishman. She is traveling with a group of upper class Brits on safari. Their encounter at a hotel bar, a wonderful scene, quickly becomes an intense love story wrapped in a harrowing journey. The episodes that follow focuse on Jake and Cara and their struggle to sustain the Dutton Ranch, confronting drought, an ongoing battle for grazing rights, and encroaching sheepherders. And there is the ruthless, amoral, wealthy Donald Whitfield (Timothy Dalton), intent on acquiring mineral-rich land including Yellowstone.

articles.text: It’s 1926. The setting for The Danish Girl is Copenhagen, Denmark. Two artists, Einar Wegener (Eddie Redmayne) and his wife, Gerda (Alicia Vikander), married some six years, live a contented, bohemian life, both in search of galleries that will carry their work. Einar, a landscape painter, is finding more success than Gerda, who has thus far confined herself to portraits of wealthy burghers. Their connection, through touch and gaze, reflects a sustained intimacy, revealing in countless subtle ways a relationship that they both cherish as they stand before easels, working, basking in the soft early morning Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander in The Danish Girl light, or reveling in the luminescent glow of late afternoon that filters through the diaphanous curtains of their bedroom. Looking out the wood-framed windows of their starkly furnished flat is a view of a busy harbor filled with working boats, their cinnabar and white sails often partially raised, swaying ever so slightly in the wind. The Danish Girl is replete with achingly gorgeous moments, not only between Einar and Gerda, but horizons framed by pink sunsets and bucolic hills obscured by orange and red wildflowers, each image suffused with color and beauty. Together they share life’s continuum, a kaleidoscope of small and not so small changes. But the depth and breath of their marriage, a touching and visible bond, is seemingly inviolable.
articles.title: The Danish Girl a fascinating journey into the unknown

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky Castle in the Sky is a swashbuckling, Indiana Jones steampunk adventure that also manages to weave into its narrative a subtle ecological message. But above all it’s for kids and there are few slow moments. From the get-go, the story is gripping and in the first opening scenes there’s a kidnapping attempt of a young orphan girl Sheeta (Anna Paquin) by a secret, nefarious agent called Muska (Mark Hamil). She is flown via airship to a military fortress, but on the way the ship is attacked by a cohort of air pirates, led by captain Dola (Cloris Leachman). The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on gratuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Nan Wright Winn died on February 24, 2025 in Waltham, MA. Born Nancy True Phillips on March 21, 1935 in Annapolis, MD, she was the daughter of Rear Admiral Richard Helsden Phillips and Betty Mackenzie Seaman Phillips. Due to her father’s career in U.S. Naval Intelligence, she traveled extensively throughout Britain and Europe as a young child. When her parents divorced in 1947, she began attending boarding schools in the U.S. & Switzerland, finally settling in at St. Agnes Episcopal School in Alexandria, VA, and graduated from their high school in 1953. During this period, her mother married Hal James Wright who became President of Creole Petroleum Corporation (Standard Oil) in Caracas, Venezuela. Traveling to and from South America as a minor became an issue, due to her last name being different from her parents, so the U.S. State Dept changed her name to Nan Wright. When attending St. Agnes, she became a Girl Scout and earned the highest award at the time, the Curved Bar. Scouting made an impact on Nan where she was a Scout leader multiple times and cultivated a life of service to others. She was a Lifetime member of the Girl Scouts. Always unconventional, her planned debutante presentation was cancelled because, unknown to her parents, in January 1957 she signed up as a commissioned Naval officer (Ensign) prior to her graduation in June 1957 from Mills College in Oakland. As a Lieutenant, she was an Occupational Therapist in the USNR Medical Service Corps with Top Secret clearance. She was an Maynard, MA. She worked as an occupational therapist, specializing in geriatric rehabilitation. She presented papers as a speaker at several worldwide OT conferences. She was a member of the American Occupational Therapy Association & the British Occupational Therapy Association. Every ancestral generation of her family has chosen to serve their country by active duty as naval officers since 1742 in the U.S. & Great Britain. After moving to MA to be near her cousins, she joined the National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution where she found a welcome group of friends. She held the position of State Chair DAR Service to Veterans, in addition to frequently acting as a liaison for the NSDAR Old Concord Chapter to the Edith Nourse Rogers Memorial Veterans Hospital in Bedford, MA. She especially enjoyed making lap quilts for veterans in wheelchairs. Nan cared about volunteerism, her country, her faith, and her family. She was a parishioner at Trinity Episcopal Church, Concord, MA. Nan is survived by her daughter Sarah Elizabeth Winn Garcia and spouse Jose Garcia, son Andrew Mackenzie Winn and spouse Mirna Winn, four grandchildren, Isabel Winn, Robert Winn, William Winn and George Winn, and cousin Susan Corey and her spouse Donald Corey. She is predeceased by her grandson, Thomas Michael Garcia. Special thanks from Sarah and Andrew to Donald Corey, Peter Corey, and Brooke Corey. An interment with military funeral honors and a memorial service are pending. Nan Wright Winn died in Waltham, Massachusetts on February 24, 2025. She was 89. Carter Sunshine, spring flowers and a cheerful crowd made for a perfect morning on April 3, as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group set out in search of seasonal blooms. Spring Blooms Shine on ‘Walking on Wednesdays’ Tour The group’s mission? A 2.5- mile flower walk through Piedmont and Crocker Parks and surrounding streets, timed to catch the city’s fleeting spring blooms at their peak. The tour started at the Exedra’s vase, where tulips — though slightly past their prime — were still lovely, albeit nibbled by curious critters. From there, the group climbed Highland Avenue to the park stairs by the bus stop. Towering cherry trees along the way, cloaked in white and pink blossoms, evoked comparisons The Wednesday walkers enjoyed the cherry blossoms of Piedmont Park at the recently renovated HighlandGuilford steps. to the famed spring displays in Washington, D.C. While the origin of those trees remains unclear, members noted that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has contributed to city landscaping since 1964, including projects at the Hall Fenway, Cherry Walk, and the Community Center. Next, the group descended the steps to the circular flower bed in front of the Community Hall, where a Yulan magnolia — native to China — had finished blooming. In its place, a generous bed of pink and white tulips was still on full display. The path continued to the Cherry Walk above the Tea House, flanked by Japanese maples — another beloved feature of the city’s designated Heritage Trees. New Heritage Trees will be announced during the Park Commission’s Arbor Day celebration on April 24 at the Community Hall. The Cherry Walk led to the recently renovated Highland-Guilford steps, which now serve as a stately entrance to the Tea House, Cherry Walk and Piedmont Park. The 2023 renovation, funded in part by $82,000 from the Beautification Foundation and $5,000 from the Piedmont Garden Club, replaced old concrete and railroad ties with elegant landings and walkways. With cherry blossoms as a backdrop, the group attempted a photo — though not everyone could squeeze into the frame. The walkers then crossed Highland Avenue and headed up Sierra Avenue, where more tulips awaited. At the end of Sierra, the group crossed Sheridan Avenue, spotting chestnut trees with fading red blooms and three graceful dogwoods in nearby front yards. Turning onto Wildwood Avenue and through the Hall Fenway, they admired more cherry trees and white calla lilies — a reminder that Easter is near. Calla lilies, native to southern Africa, now grow across the globe. In Crocker Park, walkers stopped at a path-side copper beech, also called a purple beech — another Heritage Tree. Known for its deep purple leaves in spring and copper tones in fall, the tree can live 150 to 300 years. After a short stroll up Hampton Road and Sea View Avenue, the group reached the Reich family home, a seasonal floral highlight. This year’s tulips and daffodils didn’t disappoint, and a second group photo was snapped — with everyone fitting in this time. On La Salle Avenue, the group checked on a row of rhododendrons just beginning to bud — a good reason to return in a few weeks. They looped around Mandana and Crocker Avenues near the Oakland border before heading back into Piedmont, enjoying the blooms from a reverse view. It was a colorful, fragrant, and heartwarming spring morning — a floral tour through what one walker fondly called “a big park called Piedmont.” The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420- 3070 for more information. articles.text: Spruce, a male mountain lion and the 30th rescue by Oakland Zoo, was safely transported to his new home at the Birmingham Zoo on April 4. He was rescued in January along with his siblings, Fern and Thistle, and has received care from Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital and animal care staff, thanks to donor support. Spruce will now live with his new companion, Juniper, a female rescue cub. The decision to relocate Spruce to the Birmingham Zoo was based on the compatible personalities of both cubs. The future locations for Fern and Thistle have not yet been determined. Oakland Zoo partnered with the Birmingham Zoo and FedEx to transport Spruce to Memphis, Tennessee. Over the past month, animal care staff at Oakland Zoo trained Spruce using positive reinforcement techniques to help him acclimate to the crate used for travel. “He did an amazing job shifting right into the crate for his early morning flight last Friday,” said Angela Gibson, zoological manager at Oakland Zoo, who accompanied Spruce on the flight to ensure his safety and well-being. Upon arrival in Memphis, they were met by Mollye Nardi and Amy Toman, curators at Birmingham Zoo. “We are excited that a wonderful home has been found for Spruce,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. “Though we are quick to respond when called into action, we hope measures will be implemented to prevent Oakland Zoo from needing to rescue these animals so often in the future. Coexistence is essential for the survival of this species. The zoo is committed to enhancing connectivity, nurturing coexistence, and advocating for policy initiatives to protect pumas, pets and people across the Bay Area.” Spruce and Juniper have already been introduced in their nighthouse. Keepers have observed them cuddling, playing, chirping — a form of mountain lion communication — and getting to know each other. They will remain in the nighthouse while acclimating to their new environment. Once they are ready, they will move into the Birmingham Zoo’s Wojciechowski Cougar Crossing Habitat, which opened to the public on March 19. Mountain lions in California face increasing threats from vehicle collisions, wildfires and habitat encroachment. These dangers lead to more frequent human-wildlife conflict, prompting zoos such as Oakland and Birmingham to care for orphaned mountain lions. “He and Juniper have already had positive interactions under the guidance of Birmingham Zoo and Oakland Zoo animal care professionals,” said Chris Pfefferkorn, president and CEO of Birmingham Zoo. “The cougar cubs, along with two adult bobcats, now live in a new facility designed to allow the cats to explore and display natural behaviors.” For more information about the rescued cubs, Oakland Zoo’s Mountain Lion Rescue Program and the Birmingham Zoo, please see the FAQ below. Where was Spruce and his siblings found? What happened to their mother? Fern (female), Thistle (male), and Spruce (male) were found in Portola Valley, San Mateo County. California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) believes the mother of these three cubs was the same female lion hit by a car on Portola Valley Road about 0.3 miles from where Fern, Thistle, and Spruce were found. While there were many witnesses of the mountain lion after it was hit, the carcass has since disappeared and is still being investigated. Why can’t the cubs be released to the wild? In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because Fern, Thistle, and Spruce are so young, they lacked those skills and could not be returned to the wild. How are new homes for mountain lions rescued by Oakland Zoo chosen? CDFW selects locations with the animals’ welfare and wellbeing in mind. The Zoo cares for the cubs and then assists CDFW with transporting them to appropriate institutions. Why couldn’t the cub trio be introduced to Oakland Zoo’s resident mountain lions? Many factors are considered when introducing animals – personalities, age, AZA’s Species Survival Plan recommendations, etc.– and all decisions are made with the animal’s welfare and wellbeing in mind. The trio was determined not to be the perfect match for Oakland Zoo’s resident mountain lions and Briar, another rescued puma the Zoo is caring for. According to the book’s cover, the boys said yes — but added, “we’re not British.” Not everyone in the group was charmed. A few found the stories overly cute or cringeworthy. One reader said the tone made them feel like a bad parent. Another thought the author was trying too hard and stopped reading after 30 pages. After about 45 minutes of discussion, Witte placed the call to Hershovitz. He confirmed that the kid dialogue was accurate — if sometimes reconstructed — and said the stories often serve as warm-up material for his university classes. Don’t expect a sequel, though. The boys, now nearing their teenage years, are more conscious of privacy. “Are you going to put this in a book?” Hank now asks when a philosophical moment arises. Still, Hershovitz isn’t done writing. His next book, How to Change the Past, is due out later this year. And Hank has clearly figured out his dad’s method: when a tough question comes up, he turns it around and asks, “What do you think?” That, says Hershovitz, is the whole point. The group wrapped up by confirming future selections: Cloudstreet by Tim Winton for May, How We Got to Now by Steven Johnson for June, and — after a presentation by Lois Price — The Immortalists by Chloe Benjamin for July. articles.text: A pair of great horned owls have taken up residence in Dracena Park. The Piedmont Park Commission is inviting community members to share ideas to name a pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. Suggestions may be submitted online at piedmont.ca.gov/DracenaOwls. The winning names will be selected by members of the Park Commission and announced at the City’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration on Thursday, April 24, 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Wildlife: part of a healthy park ecosystem Piedmont’s parks don’t just support people – they are shared spaces where local wildlife find shelter, food, and nesting grounds. Owls nesting in City parks is a sign of a healthy, thriving ecosystem. Owls play an important role in balancing the local environment, helping manage rodent populations naturally and maintaining ecological harmony. The owl-naming contest invites community members to connect more deeply with the natural world. Especially for kids and families, giving the owls a name can encourage curiosity about all the wildlife supported by Piedmont’s urban forest, which is home to raptors, songbirds, pollinators, and more. Forming connections with wildlife at a young age can spark a lifelong interest in conservation and stewardship. For more information, contact Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov.

Continuing on the Quarry Trail just 0.2 from the Mazzariello Labyrinth overlook, off of the trail is another labyrinth. Trail marker No. 5 on the tour is the second-largest labyrinth off of Volcanic Trail and look for trail marker No. 5. When you reach a fork in the road—with the Quarry Trail on the left—head to the right to take a slight uphill walk towards the pit. This one has a smaller heart shaped labyrinth but also nearly vertical chunk of lava sticking out of the north end of the quarry. This pit was also created by the removal of massive basalt lava from the area. In addition to dog walking, it is a great place to spark your child’s interest in geology. It also won’t be too taxing on their legs given the trail contains minor uphill portions. The park features a large parking lot with free parking and a visitor’s center that displays various types of volcanic rocks and clean restrooms. Countless super blooms of California poppies are currently ongoing with different areas occurring for the next couple of months, making it a perfect time to do research on more super blooms occurring in the surrounding areas.
